narrative:
Mara found Iven beneath the collapsed stair, one hand clamped over the wound in his side and the other still wrapped around the stolen ledger. The patrol’s lanterns moved across the courtyard below. They had come for him; if they found him here, they would find her soon after.

“You have an impressive talent for choosing the room with the fewest exits,” Mara said. Her voice held its usual dry edge, though she could hear the fear tightening it.

Iven looked at the blood on her sleeve. “You’re hurt.”

“Only in the sense that you are inconvenient.”

She could leave him. The ledger would clear her name, or most of it. His capture would end the pursuit before dawn. Instead, she took the ledger from his fingers and tucked it inside her coat. Then she drew her knife—not toward him, but toward the rope binding his ankle to the broken stone.

Iven caught her wrist. “Why?”

“Because I dislike unfinished transactions.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No. It is a price.” She pulled free. “I get you out through the cistern. You give me the ledger when we reach the river. You do not ask what happened at Greybridge, and you do not tell anyone that I was there.”

His grip tightened on the ledger’s absent place. “You expect me to trust you?”

“I expect you to recognize a bargain when it is the only door left.”

The patrol halted below. Someone called Iven’s name. Mara pressed her palm over his mouth, then waited until the footsteps moved on. Her hand remained there a moment too long—not tenderness, not quite, but an apology with nowhere safe to go.

When she removed it, he said, quietly, “Greybridge was not your fault.”

Her face did not change. “Then you have nothing to confess.”

He studied her, understood the refusal, and gave a single reluctant nod. He let her cut the rope. The choice cost Mara the clean escape she had prepared: she had to carry him through the flooded passage, leave her blood-marked coat behind, and surrender the route that could have saved her alone. Iven resisted every step, but he stopped trying to pull away. At the cistern grate, he handed her the ledger before she asked.

“This is not forgiveness,” he said.

“Good. I would hate to owe you something sentimental.”

He opened the grate. “You owe me the truth.”

“Conditional cooperation,” Mara said. “Let us not become reckless.”

They slipped into the dark together, distrust intact, but no longer useless.
title: The Price of Leaving
